faq.a: Insulin drives potassium into cells; low serum potassium can cause life‑threatening arrhythmias.
faq.q: Why is potassium checked before starting insulin?

faq.q: Can oral hypoglycaemic agents be used in DKA?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, abdominal pain and glucose 480 mg/dL – what is your immediate management and why? — Recognise DKA, give IV regular insulin, replace fluids and potassium, monitor pH.

Explain how infection with TB can alter insulin requirements in a diabetic patient – what physiologic changes occur? — Inflammation increases insulin resistance via cytokines, raises counter‑regulatory hormones, and may precipitate hyperglycaemia.

A patient on basal‑bolus insulin develops a serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/L – what steps do you take before continuing insulin? — Stop insulin, give potassium replacement until >3.3 mmol/L, then restart insulin cautiously.

Why is regular (short‑acting) insulin preferred over rapid‑acting analogues for DKA in a low‑resource setting? — Regular insulin is inexpensive, widely available, and its pharmacokinetics are well studied for continuous infusion.

Distinguish between hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state and DKA in a patient with glucose 650 mg/dL – what key investigations differentiate them? — Check serum ketones and arterial pH; HHS has minimal ketones and pH >7.3.

A pregnant woman with gestational diabetes is on oral metformin but glucose rises to 210 mg/dL – what is the next step? — Initiate insulin therapy (basal‑bolus) because oral agents are less reliable in pregnancy and risk fetal overgrowth.

How can herbal remedies common in East Africa interfere with insulin therapy? — Some herbs contain hypoglycaemic compounds that can cause unexpected lows when combined with insulin, requiring closer glucose monitoring.
What are the warning signs of insulin‑induced hypoglycaemia that require urgent care? — Altered mental status, seizures, loss of consciousness, or cardiac arrhythmia.
ai.title: Insulin Therapy in Diabetes
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Insulin replaces deficient endogenous hormone, controls hyperglycaemia and prevents acute complications. Understanding its physiology, indications, and safe use is essential for low‑resource settings.

b: Acts via insulin receptors on muscle, fat and liver
Rapidly lowers plasma glucose by facilitating cellular uptake
Deficiency or resistance leads to diabetes mellitus
sections.p: Insulin is a peptide hormone secreted by pancreatic β‑cells that promotes glucose uptake, inhibits hepatic glucose production and regulates lipid and protein metabolism.

b: Absolute insulin deficiency → type 1 diabetes, pancreatic disease, severe malnutrition
Relative deficiency with high insulin resistance → advanced type 2, infection, HIV, TB, malaria
sections.p: Clinically insulin is used when endogenous secretion is insufficient (type 1 diabetes, advanced type 2, gestational diabetes, steroid‑induced hyperglycaemia) or when oral agents fail.

t.b: Is the patient hyperglycaemic? ≥200 mg/dL confirms diabetes in symptomatic patients
Detects uncontrolled hyperglycaemia; presence of ketones suggests insulin deficiency
Shows chronic control; ≥6.5 % supports diabetes diagnosis

b: DKA: treat with regular insulin infusion, monitor glucose and electrolytes
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: high‑dose regular insulin required
Pregnant women: basal‑bolus regimen to avoid fetal macrosomia
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, insulin is often the only option to treat diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and severe hyperglycaemia, and to bridge periods of infection or pregnancy.

t.b: Guides replacement before insulin; low K⁺ (<3.3 mmol/L) contraindicates insulin until corrected
Detects metabolic acidosis in DKA; pH <7.3 confirms DKA
Tracks response to insulin; aim 150‑200 mg/dL after initial bolus

b: Explain why insulin is mandatory in DKA regardless of oral drug availability
Describe the ‘rule of 15’ for hypoglycaemia management
Identify causes of insulin resistance common in East Africa (infection, malnutrition, herbal remedies)
sections.p: Examiners test understanding of insulin’s mechanism, when to start, how to monitor, and pitfalls in low‑resource settings.

b: Starting insulin with serum K⁺ <3.3 mmol/L without replacement can precipitate cardiac arrest
Assuming normal glucose in a patient on insulin means adequate control; missed hypoglycaemia is common
Using only short‑acting insulin for basal needs leads to glucose variability
sections.p: Errors often arise from dosing misconceptions, ignoring potassium status, and misinterpreting lab results.

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained loss of consciousness (possible severe hypoglycaemia)
Persistent vomiting with high glucose (>300 mg/dL) – risk of DKA
Signs of cardiac arrhythmia after insulin initiation
